About us
The Dickson Poon School of Law, King's College London is one of the oldest law schools in England and recognised globally as one of the best law schools in the world. The School was established in 1831 and has played an integral role in the life of King's since the university was formed almost 200 years ago.​​​​​​​
The School is based in the East Wing of Somerset House on King's Strand Campus in London. Our location means that we are in the heart of legal London with the Houses of Parliament, government departments, the Royal Courts of Justice, the Inns of Court and the offices of global law firms all within walking distance.
About the role
We are recruiting a Post Doctoral Research Associate (PDRA) to work within the Centre for Data Futures (CDF) at King’s College London, in close collaboration with Prof Yulan He (KCL computer science) and her NLP group.
The post is central to the NAVIGATE research programme, which investigates how different modes of AI uncertainty expression affect the quality of human reasoning – specifically the capacity for genuine engagement with views that differ from one’s own (what the programme terms “doxastic plasticity”). The programme develops and deploys LLM-based systems in morally loaded professional contexts, including healthcare, law and education, and asks: what scaffolding strategies preserve the kind of deliberative openness required for collective norm-refinement?

Job Summary
48 Thoughts Per Minute by The Paper Birds. Co-Written with Jessica Fostekew. A co-production with New Wolsey Theatre. Co-commissioned by Corn Exchange Newbury & Warwick Arts Centre. Funded by Arts Council England, Essex County Council and The Fowler Smith Jones Trust.
Job Description
The Paper Birds are looking for professional actors for our upcoming national tour of 48 Thoughts Per Minute.
The performers will play the below named characters, as well as multi-rolling across several additional roles within the production. This is a highly visual and often physical show where the performers move in and out of acting and non-acting, converse with the audience and are active stage hands as the show portrays a range of internal experiences.
For the role of "Dan": Male actor, playing age mid-late 30s, of Black or South Asian heritage.
Dan is the life partner to the main character Tash. Dan is slightly younger than Tash and the couple are currently undergoing IVF together. Likeable and laid-back Dan is deeply in love with Tash. He lives in the moment and is often too busy coping with his own hectic mind to worry about the past or future.
Dan appears in Act 1 in Tash's mind as she remembers various comical and loving moments with him. In Act 2, the audience are welcomed into Dan's head, where they see his busy mind and hidden thoughts brought to life.
The show explores what family and friendships look like in Britain today: in all their different, complicated and wonderful forms. We are keen to build a cast that reflects the rich diversity of modern British families and communities, bringing a range of lived experiences and backgrounds to the world of the play.
Please see the attached job pack for further details

title: Research Associate  (Fixed Term)
description:
The University of Cambridge wishes to appoint a post-doctoral scientist to join the research group of Professor Suzanne Turner in the Department of Pathology. We are searching for a highly motivated scientist to investigate mechanisms of drug resistance in paediatric cancers.
Neuroblastoma is a rare childhood cancer of the peripheral nervous system that has a poor prognosis particularly for children diagnosed with high-grade disease. Our research seeks to understand why this is the case with a particular focus on drug resistance mechanisms and the development of novel biomarkers to identify poor prognosis patients. In particular, this project funded by the Little Princess Trust is looking at post-translational histone modifications towards novel therapeutic approaches and associated biomarkers towards clinical application. The ideal candidate would have knowledge of cancer biology and experience of molecular biology techniques as well as experience in supervising PhD students.
Candidates must have a PhD in biological sciences, and a track record of research achievements. Knowledge of molecular biology techniques including chromatin immunoprecipitation and sequencing are essential. We seek collegiate applicants who are committed to fostering a positive and inclusive research culture.
Fixed-term: The post is available for 6 months (with the possibility of an extension) in the first instance with a negotiable starting date and subject to a 6-month probationary period.
Once an offer of employment has been accepted, the successful candidate will be required to undergo a health assessment.
Please ensure that you upload your Curriculum Vitae (CV), a motivation letter detailing project and career development plans and include a publications list in the upload section of the online application. description:
The newly created K. Lisa Yang (KLY) Centre for Autism Research at Cambridge seeks to appoint an outstanding Assistant Research Professor (Grade 9) to lead the Autism and Early Development Research Programme within the KLY Centre.
This is an exceptional opportunity for an ambitious researcher to establish and develop an internationally recognised programme of research focused on autism and early development, investigating how prenatal, perinatal, genetic, biological and environmental factors contribute to autism and related neurodevelopmental outcomes. Working across large-scale population registers and birth cohorts in the UK, Sweden, Israel, Norway and Denmark, the postholder will help integrate genetic, clinical, epidemiological, biomarker and early developmental data to develop innovative autism likelihood scores that can support earlier identification and intervention. The programme combines cutting-edge population health research, machine learning, developmental neuroscience and translational science, with the ultimate goal of improving the early detection of autism and ensuring that children and families can access assessment, diagnosis and support at the earliest possible stage. The successful candidate will work within a highly collaborative international network and contribute to research with both fundamental scientific importance and clear potential for real-world clinical impact. The successful candidate will have the opportunity to shape the scientific direction of the programme and develop innovative lines of enquiry aligned with the strategic goals of the KLY Centre.
The successful candidate will provide scientific leadership for the Autism and Early Development Research Programme and contribute to the strategic development of the KLY Centre. As part of the leadership role, they will supervise postdoctoral researchers, develop collaborations, and lead grant development. Eligible applicants should have (1) a PhD in Psychology, Psychiatry, Neuroscience

title: Research Assistant/Associate in NanoBio Printing and Assembly (Fixed Term)
description:
A position exists for a Research Assistant/Associate in NanoBio Printing and Assembly in the Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge, to work on a multidisciplinary research programme developing protein-guided, droplet-based routes to architected functional materials, as part of an Advanced Research + Invention Agency-funded project, subject to contract negotiations. The post holder will be located in West Cambridge, Cambridgeshire, UK.
The project, collaborating across seven research groups, delivers a new pathway and manufacturing process towards multi-functional architected materials across length scales, studying:
(i) how to create rare-earth free magnetic materials at scale and in useful formats
(ii) how to create advanced, nanoporous electrodes for high capacity, long-life battery technologies
The appointee will take ownership of instrumented printing, droplet-generation, membrane-emulsification and controlled-flow systems. They will integrate protein-containing formulations, compare magnetic, electric, shear, flow and drying-assisted alignment, and test protein retention or removal to lock anisotropic order into stable materials. They will define process windows, interrogate data, maintain reproducible standard operating procedures, and support quality control and scale-up.
The role involves close collaboration across protein, mineralisation, nanocrystal, chemistry, magnetics, AI and manufacturing teams. The role also includes supporting the project lead as a technical project lead, which includes aspects of project management, coordination, risk management and mentoring.
Applicants must have obtained, or be close to obtaining, a PhD in chemical engineering, materials science or materials engineering, applied physics, fluid mechanics, colloid or interface science, or a closely related discipline, with additional expertise in biotechnology.
Essential capabilities include strong experimental skills and transferable experience in one or more printing,

title: Assistant Research Professor (Software Engineer) (Fixed Term)
description:
Join us at the world-leading CRUK Cambridge Institute. We're a unique department of the University of Cambridge, core funded by Cancer Research UK's charitable activities, and we're eagerly searching for an Assistant Research Professor with a background in software engineering to join us in a unique role.
Embedded in the Institute's Markowetz research group, the Assistant Research Professor role will lead critical software engineering research projects in support of the Institute's AI research strategy, and as part of the wider cross-Institutional CRUK AI Alliance.
The CRUK AI Alliance will link all four CRUK institutes and partners through shared infrastructure, data and expertise. The Alliance will build foundation models spanning genotype, molecular regulatory networks and tumour-organ interactions, factoring in age, sex and environmental exposure. These models will let federated teams study disease processes that can't be observed directly, such as pre-cancerous lesions, dormant residual disease and tumour-organ interactions. The Alliance will pursue questions such as: What drives cancer initiation, and how can it be intercepted to prevent disease? How can we infer patient states that can't currently be measured? How do we deliver precision healthcare? By pairing shared AI infrastructure with question-focused workstreams, the Alliance aims to make the UK cancer research ecosystem more cohesive and powerful, enabling approaches beyond the reach of current methods.
Principal responsibilities will include:
Evaluate new and existing AI tools and software for relevance and fit to the Institute's research needs.
Build, adapt and integrate selected AI tools into the Institute's existing systems and workflows.
Test and validate AI tool outputs against the standards required for research use.
Communicate the capabilities and limitations of AI tools clearly to non-specialist researchers.
Guide the Institute in adopting good practice around AI tool use and software develop

Job Summary
Tilted is looking for an Investment & Portfolio Analyst to run the numbers behind one of the UK’s largest theatre investment portfolios — modelling new shows from the producer’s pack, keeping every model, the database and the dashboard current, and owning the monthly report to investors.
Job Description
Tilted is a production company founded by producer and director Sam Hodges, making new work across theatre, live podcasts and film - recent productions include Shadowlands, Uncanny: Fear of the Dark, Every Brilliant Thing and Giant. With tech entrepreneur and investor Simon Nixon, Tilted also runs one of the UK's largest and most active theatre investment portfolios: over 100 productions backed in five years across the West End, Broadway, touring and international markets. We're building an investment process that is more systematic and more scalable - better data, proper portfolio tracking, less manual work, and automation and AI where they help. Nobody in theatre has a settled way of doing this yet; this role is at the centre of how we do it.
You will own the operational engine of the portfolio: modelling each investment opportunity from the producer's pack, keeping every model, the database and the vintage files accurate and current, tracking each show against forecast, overseeing investment cashflows, and producing the monthly and quarterly reporting that investment decisions rest on. You will also look after the tools behind the numbers - an investment database, a dashboard and a modelling app, much of it finessed with AI - and use AI in your day-to-day work. Once the cycles are running well, we expect the role to grow into helping shape how Tilted makes its strategic investment decisions, using the data you keep.

title: Research Associate (Fixed Term)
description:
How do mutant clones compete in healthy tissues as animals age, and how do some mammals suppress cancer across remarkably different lifespans and body sizes? The Cagan Lab is recruiting a Postdoctoral Research Associate to investigate these questions through comparative somatic genomics.
The Cagan Lab uses natural variation across species as a powerful experiment. Mammals differ dramatically in lifespan, body size, life history and cancer incidence. Comparing them can reveal the general rules of clonal evolution, expose lineage-specific solutions to cancer suppression, and provide a principled way to interpret emerging findings from human tissues.
This pioneering project will map age-related clonal dynamics across mammals with diverse lifespans and body-sizes including rodents, elephants and cetaceans. The aim is to uncover principles governing somatic evolution in mammals. Comparing somatic and germline tissues will reveal how clones arise and expand, which genes and pathways are selected, and how tissue context and species biology influence these processes.
The role is predominantly computational, with an experimental data-generation component and substantial intellectual ownership. You will combine high-depth error-corrected sequencing (NanoSeq), species-specific targeted gene panels, histology and quantitative evolutionary analysis. The balance of computational and experimental work will vary as the project develops.
Key responsibilities
Develop reproducible genomic workflows; call and quality-control somatic variants; quantify mutation rates and signatures; infer clone sizes and dynamics; and test for selection.
Design targeted gene panels and comparative analyses accounting for species, tissue, age, sex and sampling structure. Model clonal growth in relation to lifespan, body size, tissue architecture and cancer risk, including comparisons with human datasets.

title: Post Doctoral Research Associate: Custom Optical Microscopy Development (Fixed Term)
description:
Fixed-term: The funds for this post are available for 18 months in the first instance, if project milestone targets are met at 18 months, a further 18 months of funding will be allocated.
Applications are invited for a Postdoctoral Research Associate (PDRA) to develop custom optics integrated with microfluidic ultra-high-throughput screening (uHTS) for label free screening of phase separation in de novo designed inorganic-protein hybrid materials. Techniques developed include polarised optical microscopy (POM), fluorescence microscopy, and darkfield microscopy, coupled to droplet microfluidics for screening for libraries of 10K to >1M samples. Scientific objectives are to map the phase space of ordered inorganic hybrid materials. Screens will explore the multidimensional parameter sampling of reaction conditions and libraries of de novo inorganic-templating interfaces. The PDRA will be hosted in the group of Professor Knowles in the Department of Chemistry at Cambridge University, funded by an Advanced Research + Invention Agency (ARIA) international consortium.
The PDRA will be responsible for designing, assembling, and maintaining microscopes which integrate polarisation-resolved and fluorescence optics with existing custom microfluidic droplet screening platforms including PhaseScan and cell free expression.
Training in microfluidics will be provided. The Knowles group brings expertise in droplet-based screening, soft matter physics, biophysics, and phase separation, and the post holder is not expected to arrive with that background. Consortium partners bring expertise in de novo protein design and high-throughput inorganic synthesis. Collaborating closely with these partners, the PDRA will design, build, and utilise systems to enable uHTS to be extended to de novo designed inorganic-protein composites, identifying and optimising conditions which produce functional hybrid materials.

title: Research Associate: Behaviour and Evolution Group (Fixed Term)
description:
A Research Associate post is available in the Behaviour and Evolution Group directed by Rufus Johnstone in the Department of Zoology at the University of Cambridge.
The applicant will join an exciting, inter-disciplinary team investigating the role of intergroup conflict in the evolution of animal societies. Informed by data collected from banded mongoose and termite study systems, the applicant will develop new theoretical models of intergroup conflict, as part of an ERC Advanced Grant (INTERGROUP) awarded to Rufus Johnstone and Michael Cant and funded by the UKRI under the Horizon Guarantee programme.
Intergroup conflict is recognised as a potentially powerful force shaping the evolution of social behaviour in animal societies. However, we have limited theory to explain and predict when intergroup fights will break out, how long they will last, how they end, or their consequences for individual behaviour and life history. This successful applicant will address these questions by developing new theoretical models of conflict initiation,
dynamics, and consequences for life history allocation. The goal of the modelling work is to generate predictions that can be tested using data from the mongoose and termite systems or published data in other taxa.
The successful applicant will join the Behaviour and Evolution research group based in the Department of Zoology, directed by Rufus Johnstone. They will form part of the larger group of researchers working on the INTERGROUP project based at the universities of Exeter, Swansea, Liverpool John Moores and York. They will participate in regular meetings with the team, with potential opportunities for collaboration and short visits as the project develops. Candidates will be highly motivated and keen to interact with other components of the wider project. title: Technical Analyst
description:
The Aviation Impact Accelerator (AIA) at the University of Cambridge seeks to recruit Technical Analyst who will be based at the Whittle Laboratory in West Cambridge. The research carried out by the AIA is critically dependent upon robust modelling and analysis to support its mission of transforming aviation toward a net-zero future. This role has been created to align with the design and delivery of innovative tools and services that underpin cutting-edge research in sustainable aviation.
To assist the AIA in achieving its objectives, you will develop and operate models that assess the economic and environmental outcomes of aviation systems. You will also contribute to external reports and grant proposals under the supervision of the line manager, while engaging with stakeholders across academia, industry, and policy domains to ensure impactful delivery of research outputs.
The Aviation Impact Accelerator (AIA) uses a combination of physics-based and data-driven modelling to develop its first-order models of the aviation sector and beyond. These models compose to create a single comprehensive systems-of-systems model. In contrast to most academic modelling, we lean heavily on functional programming as a paradigm as this, along with computer algebra, immutability, and more, allows the computational implementations of our models to align more closely with their mathematics. The AIA's modelling toolboxes (there is broadly one per aviation system being modelled) are written in modern typed Python. About 90% of our current software development is greenfield, meaning that everyone helps shape the architecture of, and idioms used in, our codebases.
You will have an undergraduate degree in STEM (engineering, mathematics, physics, environmental sciences, or a related field), or equivalent practical experience. You will possess strong software skills preferably in Python, alongside proficiency in modelling and data analysis. Excellent verbal and written communication skills

title: Research Associate (Honorary Resident Doctor) in Respiratory Medicine
description:
Cambridge-GSK Translational Immunology Collaboration (CG-TIC)
We seek a highly motivated Research Associate (Honorary Resident Doctor) to contribute to cutting-edge research that will provide novel insights into the pathogenesis of respiratory disease, with a particular emphasis on collaborative work with the Cambridge-GSK Translational Immunology Collaboration (
https://www.med.cam.ac.uk/cg-tic
). This is a new interdisciplinary partnership between the University of Cambridge, Cambridge University Hospital and Royal Papworth Hospital NHS Trusts and GSK, bringing together expertise from these partners.
The Research Associate (Honorary Resident Doctor) will conduct high-quality research as part of a clinical cohort research study that is using endophenotyping and laboratory studies to investigate respiratory disease mechanisms in Interstitial Lung Diseases. In the clinical cohort research study, the research associate will provide clinical support, covering a weekly research clinic and bronchoscopy list. The lab studies will include integration of multi-omics and clinical data and will involve close collaboration with colleagues across CG-TIC and at GSK.

title: Postdoctoral Research Associate - Bhatia Group (Fixed Term)
description:
A post-doctoral Research Associate position is available in the Bhatia group at the Sainsbury Laboratory Cambridge University. Successful candidates will conduct fundamental research investigating the mechanistic basis of the function of the plant hormone cytokinin in plant development using
Arabidopsis thaliana
leaves as model. This will involve
extensive time-lapse imaging
of developing leaves using confocal microscopy to elucidate how cytokinin controls the spatiotemporal distribution of cellular growth patterns underlying plant organogenesis. They will join a young, growing lab and are expected to bring energy, enthusiasm, and a proactive commitment to both developing research and positive lab culture.
The candidate will be working in a stimulating scientific environment with ample opportunities to learn new techniques. The successful candidate will be encouraged to apply for fellowships with the help of the lab.
Qualifications:
Applicants must have a recent Ph.D degree (within one-two years is desirable but not essential) with strong foundations in plant developmental biology, genetics and molecular biology.
Extensive demonstrated experience in time-lapse imaging using confocal microscopy is essential.  Expertise in imaging plant aerial organs, particularly leaves and the shoot apical meristem, is highly desirable.
Experience in quantitative imaging data analysis (using MorphoGraphX, Image J, Imaris etc.) is desirable and will be an advantage.
Experience in basic molecular biology techniques including cloning, and generation and handling of transgenic Arabidopsis plants is essential.
Excellent communication skills in both oral and written English are expected.
Successful candidates will be expected to work collaboratively in the lab.
Strong observation skills, critical thinking, problem-solving abilities, and organisational and record-keeping skills are essential.
The ability to work independently and take proactive measures when needed is essential.

description:
We are seeking a talented biomedical data scientist to join our team as a postdoctoral researcher in the Cardiovascular Epidemiology Unit (CEU) and Cambridge Baker Systems Genomics Initiative (CBSGI) of the Department of Public Health and Primary Care (DPHPC). The post will suit researchers interested in using artificial intelligence (AI) to create predictive models of biological processes. The ideal postholder will also have an interest or experience in analysing genomic, multi-omic and phenotypic/health-record data at population scales.
The primary role of the post holder will be to lead projects that develop new AI models, benchmark existing models and combine multiple approaches to predict biochemically important parameters. A challenge will be developing models and tools which can be applied rapidly and at scale in human populations (e.g. >1 million individuals). The post holder will also be deeply involved in the quantitative analysis and interpretation of genomic, multi-omic and phenotypic data using polygenic scores, GWAS, Mendelian randomisation, and other statistical and machine-learning methods.
The appointed researcher will have research interests aligned with those of our groups and the freedom to develop their own ideas for new research by contributing to the preparation of new grant applications. Initial possibilities for research projects include:
Leveraging biochemical knowledge and databases (e.g. REACTOME) to model and interpret multi-omics data and complex phenotypes
Integrating multi-omics data to dissect the molecular etiology of cardiometabolic diseases
Combining genetics and structural bioinformatics to understand variant-to-function and potentially improve therapeutic outcomes

Overview
The Ali Lab wishes to recruit a student to work on the project entitled: "Discovery of rational therapeutic biomarkers in breast cancer by systems pathology and deep learning".
For further information about the research group, including their most recent publications, please visit their website at
www.ali-lab.co.uk/
Project details
The therapeutic landscape for breast cancer patients is rapidly evolving with novel therapies regularly receiving regulatory approval. Yet directing these treatments to patients likely to benefit while sparing those unlikely to respond from their toxicities remains a major challenge. Many modern therapies, like immunotherapy and ADCs, rely on tissue architecture to be effective. Intercellular relationships in breast cancer tissues also determine cellular activation states and expression profiles, rendering some cells susceptible and others resistant to new treatments.
The aim of this project is to use modern multiomic spatial methods (in which our group has extensive expertise1¿4) together with deep learning (for efficient representation and cross-modal learning) to discover the potential therapeutic landscape for novel therapies in breast cancer, and to propose rational multidimensional biomarkers for combinatorial therapy. We are generating multimodal spatial datasets in cohorts of breast cancer patients (the largest of their kind; making extensive use of imaging mass cytometry and spatial transcriptomics) that span observational studies and clinical trials. We must precisely define the landscape of novel target expression, quantify its heterogeneity, and the contribution of tissue architecture as a determinant of expression profiles. Our laboratory investigates the biology of preneoplastic cell states, with particular interest in how changes in cell functional identity and plasticity are controlled by the epigenome. We are interested in how oncogenic and metabolic signalling reshapes chromatin organisation and gene regulation, how these changes influence cellular fitness and tissue microenvironment, and which states ultimately suppress or promote tumour development.
The PhD project will investigate the molecular and epigenetic mechanisms underlying transitions between preneoplastic cell states using diverse models, both in vitro and in vivo. The precise direction of the project will be developed according to the student's interests and emerging findings in the laboratory. Depending on the specific questions addressed, approaches may include mammalian cell culture, molecular and cell biology, genetic perturbation, imaging, epigenetic and chromatin profiling, and in vivo models of early tumorigenesis. Genomic and single-cell approaches may also be used, supported by collaboration with computational scientists.

For further information about the research group, including their most recent publications, please visit their website at
https://biffilab.wordpress.com
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains a formidable clinical challenge. A major recent advance has been the development of KRAS inhibitors, which have shown considerable promise in clinical trials (1). For decades, KRAS was considered undruggable; however, these new inhibitors represent a potential turning point for patients with PDAC. Despite this progress, rapid therapy resistance has already been observed in both patients and pre-clinical mouse models, highlighting the urgent need to define the mechanisms that drive resistance and to identify rational combination therapies.
In our laboratory, we have established and validated a panel of genetically heterogeneous PDAC models. These studies have shown that malignant-cell genetics shape distinct, therapeutically actionable vulnerabilities through both cell-intrinsic programmes and changes in the surrounding tumour microenvironment [(2) and unpublished]. These observations create an important opportunity: we hypothesise that malignant¿stromal crosstalk within defined genetic contexts drives distinct mechanisms of resistance to KRAS inhibition. In support of this, our work indicates that cancer-associated fibroblasts play diverse roles in PDAC progression and activate pathways that may contribute to therapy resistance (3, 4). This PhD project will therefore identify malignant cell-intrinsic and malignant cell-extrinsic mechanisms of resistance to KRAS inhibition, including fibroblast-mediated mechanisms, across genetically distinct PDACs. We will prioritise PDAC genotypes for which we already have preliminary data suggesting candidate mechanisms of resistance.

title: Research Associate - Miska Group (Fixed Term)
description:
The research team of Professor Eric Miska is recruiting a postdoctoral associate in the area of RNA biology.
We are an international, supportive and collaborative research group. Most of our ongoing research projects fall under one of these broader themes: RNA modifications and structure; Small-and non-coding RNA biology; RNA in communication and defense; Genomics, epigenomics, and Inheritance; Adaptive plasticity and evolution. Our projects span miRNA biology and pathology, miRNA mechanisms, piRNA biology and the germline, endo-siRNAs in epigenetic inheritance and environmental conditioning, small RNA evolution, and the role of RNAi in host pathogen interactions.
We are part of the Department of Biochemistry at the University of Cambridge and are affiliated with the Gurdon Institute and the Wellcome Sanger Institute. We have access to state-of-the-art facilities for experimental and computational work.
We are looking for a new team member to work on the role of RNA modification and structure in RNA function.
A suitable candidate will have completed a PhD in a relevant subject, has demonstrated research impact and has experience in working with RNA.

title: Research Associate (Blouet and Káradóttir Labs)
description:
Oligodendrocyte progenitor cells are now recognised as stem cells of the adult brain, recruited for learning and repair throughout life. This project aims at testing innovative ways of recruiting oligodendrocyte lineage cells in neurodegenerative disease by targeting metabolic pathways.
This post is part of a new collaborative research programme at the University of Cambridge based across the laboratories of Professor Clémence Blouet (Institute of Metabolic Science) and Professor Ragnhildur Thóra Káradóttir (Cambridge Stem Cell Institute; Director of the MS Society Cambridge Centre for Myelin Repair). The project is funded by Eli Lilly and will test the idea that targeting incretin receptor agonists can promote remyelination and support brain repair in progressive multiple sclerosis.
The successful candidate will work across both laboratories. The project will involve focal demyelinating lesion models, stereotaxic surgery and pharmacological interventions, in vivo recordings of neuronal activity, histology and imaging, and single-nucleus transcriptomics.
This is a unique opportunity to work at the interface of metabolic science and neuroscience in a collaborative translational environment, with access to state-of-the-art facilities across the Cambridge Stem Cell Institute, the Institute of Metabolic Science, and the wider Cambridge Biomedical Campus.
Requirements:
Applicants should hold a PhD in neuroscience or a related discipline. A strong background in in vivo rodent work is essential. Experience with several of the required techniques is important, including stereotaxic surgery, histology, imaging, or electrophysiological techniques, particularly in vivo. We will provide training where needed . The successful candidate must be highly organised, able to work both independently and collaboratively, and have strong analytical and communication skills.
